 2   Q   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A   James A. Leyko. My business address is 16690 Swingley Ridge Road, Suite 140,

 4       Chesterfield, MO 63017.



 5   Q   WHAT IS YOUR OCCUPATION?

 6   A   I am a consultant in the field of public utility regulation and a Senior Consultant

 7       with the firm of Brubaker & Associates, Inc. (“BAI”), energy, economic and

 8       regulatory consultants.



 9   Q   PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR EDUCATIONAL AND PROFESSIONAL

10       BACKGROUND.

12   Q   ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU APPEARING IN THIS PROCEEDING?

14       USA (“LES”) and the Federal Executive Agencies (“FEA”). LES and FEA own

15       and operate facilities in the Southwestern Public Service Company (“SPS” or

 1   Q   WHAT      IS   THE     PURPOSE       OF     YOUR      TESTIMONY      IN    THIS

 2       PROCEEDING?

 3   A   The purpose of my testimony is to address SPS’s claimed revenue deficiency.

 4       Specifically, I support adjustments to the Company’s revenue requirement in the

 5       following areas:

 6          •   Cash Working Capital

 7          •   Deferred Excess Liability Insurance Premiums

 8          •   Rate Case and Regulatory Expenses



 9   Q   PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR RECOMMENDATIONS AND FINDINGS.

10   A   FEA and LES recommend several adjustments to SPS’s claimed revenue

11       deficiency. As outlined in Table 1 below, I believe the Company’s claimed revenue

12       deficiency of $175.355 million is overstated by at least $54.361 million. FEA’s

13       and LES’s adjustments in Table 1 are supported by myself and my colleagues

14       Michael P. Gorman, Christopher C. Walters and Brian C. Andrews.

 1   Q   DOES THE FACT THAT YOU DID NOT ADDRESS EVERY ISSUE

 2       RAISED IN SPS’S TESTIMONY MEAN THAT YOU AGREE WITH SPS’S

 3       TESTIMONY ON THOSE ISSUES?

 4   A   No. It merely reflects that I chose not to address all those issues in my testimony.

 5       It should not be read as an endorsement of, or agreement with, SPS’s position on

 6       such issues. In addition, other parties may offer additional reasonable downward

 7       adjustments to SPS’s revenue requirement.



 8                                II. CASH WORKING CAPITAL

 9   Q   WHAT CASH WORKING CAPITAL (“CWC”) BALANCE DOES SPS PROPOSE?

10   A   SPS proposes a CWC balance of $34,605,261.1



11   Q   WHAT IS CWC?

12   A   CWC is the amount of cash necessary to finance the day-to-day operations of a

13       utility. CWC may be positive when it is shown that the utility’s shareholders

14       provide the financing for paying bills before billed revenues are collected from

15       customers, or it can be negative when customers pay the utility more promptly

16       than the utility is required to pay its bills. Broadly speaking, a CWC requirement

17       is calculated as a comparison between a revenue lag and an expense lag, also called



         1
             Attachment AMJ-BR 1(e) at 9.

                                             Page 4
                                 Direct Testimony of James A. Leyko
                                  NMPRC Case No. 25-00079-UT


 1       a lead/lag study. A lead/lag study measures the inflows and outflows of cash that

 2       a utility incurs to provide service to its customers.



 3   Q   WHAT METHODOLOGY DOES SPS PROPOSE TO QUANTIFY ITS CWC

 4       BALANCE?

 5   A   Instead of a lead/lag study, SPS proposes to use the one-eighth method. SPS

 6       witness Zoë E. Lees supports the Company’s proposal. The one-eighth method, or

 7       the 45-day formula, estimates a utility’s CWC by valuing it at one-eighth of total

 8       O&M (or 45/365 days). SPS’s New Mexico Retail O&M is $276,842,087.2

 9       Therefore, SPS estimates its CWC as $34,605,261, or $276,842,087 divided by 8.



10   Q   DO YOU HAVE ANY CONCERNS WITH THE AMOUNT OF CWC

11       REQUESTED BY SPS?

12   A   Yes. As described above, a utility’s CWC can be positive or negative. This can be

13       seen in the PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP (“PwC”) report that Ms. Lees includes as

14       Attachment ZEL-8. On page 19 of the attachment (tilted in the report as Exhibit B:

15       Cash Working Capital (“CWC”) as a Percentage of Rate Base By Method) several

16       utilities have a negative CWC balance. However, SPS’s proposed use of the one-

17       eighth method guarantees a positive CWC balance. My concern is that SPS has not



         2
             Attachment AMJ-BR 1(e) at 2.

                                             Page 5
                                  Direct Testimony of James A. Leyko
                                   NMPRC Case No. 25-00079-UT


 1       justified having a positive CWC balance because it has not performed a lead/lag

 2       study to measure SPS’s cash flows. A lead/lag study is the most common way to

 3       calculate a utility’s CWC and it is a study SPS has done in past rate cases. The

 4       PwC report shows that 22 of the 28 utilities the report reviewed use a lead/lag study.

 5       Only two utilities used a formula approach like SPS is proposing here.



 6   Q   DID SPS HAVE A NEGATIVE CWC BALANCE IN PRIOR RATE CASES?

 7   A   Yes. SPS used the same one-eighth method in its last base rate case but in both

 8       Docket Nos. 20-00238-UT3 and 19-00170-UT4 the Company had a negative CWC

 9       balance. In both cases the Company measured its CWC using a lead/lag study.

10       SPS has not justified having a positive CWC balance in this case because the

11       Company has not measured its CWC, only estimated it via a formula nor has the

12       Company shown that its CWC would no longer be negative if it was measured via

13       a lead/lag study.



14   Q   WHAT EVIDENCE DID SPS PROVIDE TO SUPPORT ITS POSITIVE

15       CWC?

16   A   The only evidence SPS witness Zoe Lees provides beyond the fact that two other

17       utilities in the PwC report also used a formula approach, was that CWC is typically


         3
             Case No. 20-00238-UT, Freitas Schedule E-1, page 2.
         4
             Case No. 19-00170-UT, Freitas Schedule E-1, page 2.

                                               Page 6
                                   Direct Testimony of James A. Leyko
                                    NMPRC Case No. 25-00079-UT


 1          0.83% of the utility’s rate base (according to the PwC report).5 SPS argues their

 2          request is in line with this average. “SPS requests a CWC of approximately $22.7

 3          million, which is 0.93% of rate base. This is in line with the average of 0.83% in

 4          Exhibit E of the PwC report.”6 However, all this shows is that PwC found that

 5          utilities, on average, have a positive CWC balance. SPS provided no evidence that

 6          it should have a positive CWC balance in this case. Again, SPS calculated a

 7          negative CWC balance in both Docket Nos. 20-00238-UT and 19-00170-UT and

 8          the Company provided no evidence circumstances have changed since those studies

 9          were performed.



10   Q      IS THERE AN ALTERNATIVE TO THE FORMULA BASED APPROACH

11          THAT SPS USES IN THIS RATE CASE?

12   A      Yes. The Commission can set SPS’s ratemaking CWC to $0. This approach is

13          outlined in the PwC report that Ms. Lees cites.

14                  Zero CWC Allowance

15                  A final approach is to set the CWC allowance to zero. This can
16                  reasonably serve as a proxy for the cash working capital allowance
17                  and involves no time to create from the utility’s perspective nor its
18                  commission to review. Such an approach is based on the
19                  knowledge that different approaches can produce different results,
20                  some positive, some negative and that the CWC concept is an
21                  estimate. In some cases, the regulator may require use of a lead-

            5
            Direct Testimony of Zoë E. Lees (“Lees Direct“) at 74.
            6
            Lees Direct at 75. SPS later updated its CWC request to $34,605,261. See Attachment
     AMJ-BR 1(e), page 9.

                                                Page 7
                                 Direct Testimony of James A. Leyko
                                  NMPRC Case No. 25-00079-UT


 1                 lag approach or other method only if the utility is requesting CWC.
 2                 In effect, this is the same as a zero CWC allowance. Assigning a
 3                 zero CWC allowance recognizes the subjective nature of the
 4                 various approaches and eliminates the time and effort involved in
 5                 including, defending and deciding this rate base component.7

 6                 I recommend the Commission adopt this approach in this case given there

 7       is no lead/lag study to support SPS’s CWC. As the PwC report says, this method

 8       can serve as a proxy for a utility’s CWC when better data is not available. This

 9       method also recognizes that a utility’s CWC can be both positive or negative. This

10       is a conservative adjustment because it is possible a lead/lag study would result in

11       a negative CWC for SPS and a reduction to rate base given the lead/lag studies the

12       Company performed in Docket Nos. 20-00238-UT and 19-00170-UT resulted in

13       negative balances.



14   Q   PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR ADJUSTMENT.

15   A   I recommend the Commission set SPS’s ratemaking CWC to $0. This reduces

16       SPS’s New Mexico Retail rate base by $34,605,261. The revenue requirement

17       impact of my adjustment is approximately $3.176 million, or the $34,605,261 times

18       my colleague Mr. Walter’s proposed rate of return, grossed up for income taxes.




         7
             Attachment ZEL-8 at 12.

 1                III. EXCESS LIABILITY INSURANCE PREMIUMS

 2   Q   WHAT IS SPS’S EXCESS LIABILITY INSURANCE (“ELI”) AND WHAT

 3       DOES SPS PROPOSE REGARDING ITS ELI PREMIUMS IN THIS CASE?

 4   A   ELI is insurance that protects SPS against liabilities the Company could owe to

 5       third parties.8 SPS witness Robert L. Miller notes that Xcel Energy is the holder of

 6       SPS’s insurance policies.9 The insurance costs are then allocated or directly

 7       assigned to SPS.10 Mr. Miller argues that SPS’s ratepayers benefit from the ELI

 8       because it protects the Company from “catastrophic claims it may face while

 9       providing service for its customers.”11 Miller provides more details on SPS and

10       Xcel Energy’s ELI in his direct testimony.

11               In this proceeding SPS seeks to recover both the test year ELI premiums

12       and ELI costs that were deferred to a regulatory asset per the Commission’s Order

13       in Docket No. 25-00030-UT. SPS proposes to recover the deferred costs over two

14       years.12 Mr. Miller states the test year ELI premiums are estimated to be $45.8

15       million.13

 1   Q   PLEASE EXPLAIN WHY THE COMMISSION DIRECTED SPS TO

 2       DEFER ELI COSTS TO A REGULATORY ASSET IN DOCKET NO. 25-

 3       00030-UT.

 4   A   This can be seen in Mr. Miller’s Table RLM-1. SPS’s ELI premiums were $8.1

 5       million in 2021 and $8.0 million in 2022. Around the time the Commission issued

 6       the Final Order in SPS’s last base rate case, Docket No. 22-00286-UT, the ELI

 7       premiums increased to $11.6 million. However, in 2024 the premiums increased

 8       to $42.6 million. Mr. Miller explains that insurance premiums increased because

 9       of increased claims and higher risks due to wildfires and wildfire claims.14

10              SPS filed an application on April 7, 2025, seeking to defer the increase in

11       ELI premiums over a baseline. The Commission determined that SPS’s request

12       was in the public interest and that the ELI increase represented exceptional

13       circumstances.15 The Docket No. 25-00030-UT Order also confirmed that rate

14       recovery of the deferred costs would be addressed in this proceeding:

15              The Commission agrees that, in approving SPS’s Application, it is
16              only preserving SPS’s right to present the deferred costs for a
17              prudency review during SPS’s next rate case, and that the
18              Commission is not deeming such costs prudent now through the
19              issuance of this accounting order.16

 1   Q   WHAT IS THE TOTAL AMOUNT OF DEFERRED ELI COSTS?

 2   A   The Commission Order in Docket No. 25-00030-UT allowed SPS to defer costs

 3       through the date rates approved in this proceeding go into effect. Thus, the actual

 4       amount of deferred costs is not yet known. In SPS’s original application the

 5       Company requested a $14,105,809 test year adjustment to represent a two-year

 6       deferral of a $28,151,745 regulatory asset.17 SPS’s response to discovery request

 7       Question No. FEA 2-12 (provided in Exhibit JAL-1) the Company was asked for

 8       workpapers supporting the ELI deferral. Exhibit SPS-FEA 2-12 provided with the

 9       response to the discovery request shows the forecasted regulatory asset was

10       $26,223,655 as of February 28, 2026, or a $1,928,090 decrease from what the

11       Company originally forecasted.



12   Q   DO YOU HAVE ANY CONCERNS WITH SPS’S REQUEST TO RECOVER

13       ITS DEFERRED COSTS?

14   A   Yes. I have two concerns with SPS’s request. First, the Commission should reject

15       SPS’s request to recover these costs over two years and should instead direct the

16       Company to recover the deferred ELI costs over three years for the reasons I will




         17
              Direct Testimony of Allison M. Johnson at 102.

                                               Page 11
                              Direct Testimony of James A. Leyko
                               NMPRC Case No. 25-00079-UT


 1   address in the next section of my testimony. As explained below, SPS also

 2   requested a two-year recovery of other regulatory expenses.

 3             Second, I am concerned about SPS’s request to recover deferred ELI costs

 4   that are allocated to SPS rather than directly assigned. SPS provided a calculation

 5   of the deferred costs in response to discovery request Question No. FEA 2-12

 6   (provided in Exhibit JAL-1).         The response shows that of the $26,223,655

 7   regulatory asset balance forecasted for November 30, 2026, $3,996,778 of the

 8   balance comes from costs allocated to SPS by Xcel Energy. The remainder of the

 9   costs are directly assigned. The relative weight of directly assigned versus allocated

10   costs can also be seen in Mr. Miller’s Table RLM-1. The table shows that in 2025,

11   $5.0 million out of the $45.8 million total ELI premiums are allocated by Xcel

12   Energy.

13             In the Docket No. 25-00030-UT Order the Commission concluded that,

14   “regulatory assets and liabilities should be granted only in exceptional

15   circumstances” including situations where the amount at issue is “material.”18 Mr.

16   Miller’s Table RLM-1 shows that the increase in ELI premiums was driven

17   primarily by costs that are directly assigned to SPS. In October 2024 the monthly

18   premiums directly assigned to SPS increased from approximately $686,000 per

19   month to $3.2 million per month, over a 350% increase.19 In comparison, the ELI

 1          costs allocated to SPS increased at the same time from approximately $277,000 per

 2          month to approximately $440,000 per month.20 Again, this can be seen on Mr.

 3          Miller’s Table RLM-1.      Between 2023 and 2024 the directly assigned costs

 4          increased by $29 million while allocated costs increased by $2 million. The

 5          volatility of these allocated costs appears to be much lower than the costs directly

 6          assigned to SPS.



 7   Q      DID YOU REVIEW THE ALLOCATED ELI COSTS?

 8   A      Yes. Part of the reason these costs appear less volatile when looking at them from

 9          SPS’s perspective may be how these costs are allocated. SPS’s response to

10          discovery request Question No. FEA 2-14 (provided in Exhibit JAL-1) confirms

11          the allocation factor for these costs in 2025 was 14.4095%. This allocation factor

12          can be found on SPS’s Attachment NLD-7, attached to the Direct Testimony of

13          Nicole L. Doyle. This allocation factor is a composite based on SPS’s total assets,

14          total revenues, and number of employees. This means the allocation factor will

15          change each year. This same allocation factor was 15.7347% in March 2023.21

16          SPS’s share of these costs is dropping even as the overall cost allocated to SPS and

17          its affiliates increases. The higher allocation of these costs included in SPS’s

 1           approved rates (relative to today’s allocation factor) offsets a portion of SPS’s share

 2           of the increased cost.

 3                   I do not believe SPS has justified recovery of these costs. The accounting

 4           order approved by the Commission in Case No. 25-00030-UT was not designed to

 5           protect SPS from smaller changes in the amount of costs allocated to the Company,

 6           but rather to protect SPS from the extraordinary circumstances created by a tripling

 7           in premiums directly assigned to SPS. I recommend the Commission disallow

 8           recovery of these allocated costs.

10   A       My adjustment is shown on Exhibit JAL-2. Removing the allocated costs from

15           due to the lower regulatory asset balance the Company provided in discovery. I

16           have not made an adjustment to the $11.6 million baseline given the Order in

17           Docket No. 22-00286-UT specifically cites $11.6 million as the baseline.

 1                  In addition to my adjustment to disallow recovery of the allocated ELI costs,

 2       I also recommend the deferred ELI costs be recovered over three years.



 3              IV. THREE YEAR RECOVERY OF CERTAIN EXPENSES

 4   Q   DO YOU HAVE ANY CONCERNS WITH THE RECOVERY PERIODS SPS

 5       PROPOSES FOR CERTAIN COSTS?

 6   A   Yes. SPS proposes a two-year recovery period for rate case and regulatory

 7       expenses in this proceeding.23 For example, SPS proposes a two-year recovery of

 8       the ELI regulatory asset. SPS witness Zoë E. Lees states SPS is proposing a two-

 9       year recovery of these costs because the Company intends to file frequent rate

10       cases.

11                  A two-year amortization period is reasonable because SPS remains
12                  in a significant multi-year capital spending cycle, and during that
13                  time SPS will place numerous capital projects in service, which may
14                  make it necessary for SPS to file frequent rate cases.24

15                  Table 2, below, shows the rate case and regulatory expenses that SPS is

16       proposing to recover over two-years.

 3   Q   PLEASE EXPLAIN.

 4   A   Rate case and regulatory expenses should be recovered over the period rates

 5       approved in this proceeding will likely be in effect (if a longer recovery period is

 6       not warranted). Therefore, it is important to look at the cadence in which SPS

 7       typically files rate cases. While SPS asserts that rates approved in this proceeding

 8       will only be in effect for about two years because of its capital spending, a look at

 9       the Company’s last rate case shows that rates could be in effect for longer.

10                The Final Order in SPS’s last rate case was issued in October 2023. This

11       means rates approved in SPS’s last rate case will be in effect for about three years.

                               NMPRC Case No. 25-00079-UT


 1   If the Commission approves a two-year amortization and SPS’s rates are in effect

 2   for three years, then this will allow SPS to over-recover its approved rate case and

 3   regulatory expenses. Importantly, this has already happened.

 4             The Stipulation that settled SPS’s last rate case used a two-year amortization

 5   for rate case expense. The Stipulation reads:

 6             VI. Rate Case Expenses

 7             The stipulated base rate increase includes recovery of $2,000,000
 8             in rate case expenses to be amortized over two years. If rates in
 9             SPS’s next base rate case take effect prior to full recovery of the
10             $2,000,000, the unamortized costs from this case will not be
11             recovered from customers.25

12   While the Stipulation included a clause that prevented SPS from recovering its full

13   rate case expenses if the Company filed a rate case before two years passed, what

14   actually happened is that rates were in effect for three years which means SPS over

15   recovered its rate case expense. If the Company waits three years for its next rate

16   case, as it did before filing this rate case, then SPS will over-recover these costs. I

17   recommend the Commission direct SPS to amortize these expenses over three

18   years, consistent with how SPS filed its last two rate cases. This protects both SPS

19   and its ratepayers. If SPS filed for a rate case before three years pass, and as a result

20   the rate case and regulatory expenses were not fully recovered, then the Company

 3   Q   PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR ADJUSTMENT.

 4   A   My adjustment is included on Exhibit JAL-2. For the reasons discussed above, I

 5       recommend a three-year amortization of rate case and regulatory expenses. This

 6       adjustment lowers SPS’s revenue requirement by approximately $9.771 million

 7       (including the impact to ELI that I discussed in the prior section).26

 8                 Also, there appears to be a discrepancy between SPS witnesses Johnson and

 9       Lee regarding rate case expense. Ms. Johnson states there is $4,614,630 of deferred

10       rate case expenses. However, Attachment ZEL-7 shows there is $4,342,330. My

11       adjustment assumes Attachment ZEL-7 is the correct figure but that $4,614,630 is

12       the amount included in SPS’s $175.355 million revenue requirement.

                             Qualifications of James A. Leyko

Q      PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

A      James A. Leyko. My business address is 16690 Swingley Ridge Road, Suite 140,

Chesterfield, MO 63017.



Q      PLEASE STATE YOUR OCCUPATION.

A      I am a Senior Consultant in the field of public utility regulation with the firm of

Brubaker & Associates, Inc. (“BAI”), energy, economic and regulatory consultants.



Q      PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND AND

EXPERIENCE.

A      I received a Bachelor of Arts Degree in History from Tulane University in 2007. I

attended Saint Louis University and received a Master of Business Administration Degree in

2011. I joined BAI and served in the analyst department until 2012. Prior to rejoining BAI as

a Consultant in 2018, I worked as a Regulatory Economist for the Maryland Public Service

Commission and as the Regulatory Affairs Manager for the Efficiency Maine Trust.

       I have written testimony and appeared as an expert witness before the Illinois Commerce

Commission, the Maine Public Utilities Commission, the Maryland Public Service

Commission, and the Oklahoma Corporation Commission, and have supported filings for

several regulated utility matters as a Consultant for BAI. These assignments included revenue

requirement issues such as incentive compensation and vegetation management, income taxes,

the impact of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, and resource planning.

and negotiations, in both regulated and unregulated markets. Our clients include large industrial

and institutional customers, state regulatory agencies, and some utilities. We also prepare

special studies and reports, forecasts, surveys and siting studies, and present seminars on utility-
